solution:
In a Lewis dot diagram every valence electron is shown as a dot; a shared pair drawn between two atoms is a covalent bond, and the pairs left on an atom are its lone pairs.

**a. Hydrogen \((\mathrm{H_2})\)** — each H has one valence electron and the two atoms share them, so there is a single shared pair and no lone pair. Each hydrogen thereby attains the duplet of helium.

\(\mathrm{H}\!:\!\mathrm{H}\)  or  \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}\)

**b. Water \((\mathrm{H_2O})\)** — oxygen has 6 valence electrons and shares one with each hydrogen, giving two bonded pairs; the remaining four electrons stay on oxygen as two lone pairs. Oxygen acquires an octet and each hydrogen a duplet.

\(\mathrm{H}\!:\!\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}\!:\!\mathrm{H}\)

**c. Carbon dioxide \((\mathrm{CO_2})\)** — carbon contributes 4 electrons and each oxygen 6, and the octet on carbon is completed only by forming a double bond (two shared pairs) to each oxygen. Every oxygen keeps two lone pairs.

\(\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}\!::\!\mathrm{C}\!::\!\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}\)  or  \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\)

**d. Methane \((\mathrm{CH_4})\)** — carbon's four valence electrons are shared one with each of four hydrogens, giving four bonded pairs and no lone pair. Carbon acquires an octet, each hydrogen a duplet.

\(\mathrm{H}\!:\!\underset{\displaystyle \mathrm{H}}{\overset{\displaystyle \mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{C}}}\!:\!\mathrm{H}\)  — carbon at the centre with a shared pair to each of the four hydrogens (the pairs to the H atoms drawn above and below are not repeated in this linear rendering), i.e. the four single bonds of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\).

**e. Lithium Fluoride \((\mathrm{LiF})\)** — this one is ionic, not covalent. Lithium \((2,1)\) loses its single valence electron and fluorine \((2,7)\) gains it, exactly as the chapter shows for \(\mathrm{Na}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) in §5.2.1. The two ions are then held by electrostatic attraction:

\(\mathrm{Li}^{\oplus}\ \left[:\!\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{F}}}\!:\right]^{\ominus}\)

Fluoride carries four lone pairs and a complete octet. Lithium is left with the helium duplet — the chapter notes in §5.2 that the octet rule does not apply to H and Li, which "tend to have only two electrons in their valence shell".

In ethene each carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridized (§5.4.5 ii).

**Hybridization.** The ground state of carbon is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^1\ 2p_y^1\ 2p_z^0}\). One \(2s\) electron is promoted to the vacant \(2p\) orbital, and then the \(2s\) orbital and two of the \(2p\) orbitals mix and recast into three \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals of equal energy and shape. The three hybrids lie in one plane at \(120^\circ\) to each other; the third \(p\) orbital takes no part in hybridization and stands at right angles to that plane.

**The bonds to be drawn.**

1. Two of the three \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals on each carbon overlap axially with the \(1s\) orbital of a hydrogen atom, giving four \(sp^2\)-\(s\) \(\sigma\) bonds (two at each carbon).

2. The third \(sp^2\) hybrid on one carbon overlaps axially with the third \(sp^2\) hybrid on the other carbon, giving one \(sp^2\)-\(sp^2\) C-C \(\sigma\) bond.

3. The two unhybridized \(p\) orbitals, one on each carbon, stand parallel and perpendicular to the molecular plane; they overlap sideways (laterally) to give one \(p\)-\(p\) \(\pi\) bond, whose electron cloud lies above and below the plane of the six atoms.

So the diagram must show five \(\sigma\) bonds in one plane (four C-H and one C-C, all H-C-H and H-C-C angles about \(120^\circ\)) and, above and below that plane, the lateral overlap of the two \(p\) orbitals forming the \(\pi\) bond. The chapter states the count in these words: "the \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) molecule has four \(sp^2\)-\(s\) \(\sigma\) bonds. One \(sp^2\)-\(sp^2\) \(\sigma\) bond one \(p\)-\(p\) \(\pi\) bond." All six atoms are coplanar, which is why the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) bond cannot rotate freely.

**a. \(\mathrm{HF}\)** — hydrogen contributes 1 electron and fluorine 7. One shared pair bonds them and fluorine keeps three lone pairs, completing its octet while hydrogen attains the duplet.

\(\mathrm{H}\!:\!\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{F}}}\!:\)  or  \(\mathrm{H}-\ddot{\mathrm{F}}\!:\)

**b. \(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\)** (ethane) — each carbon shares one electron with each of three hydrogens and one with the other carbon: seven single bonds in all (six C-H and one C-C), no lone pair anywhere, octet on both carbons.

\(\mathrm{H_3C}\!:\!\mathrm{CH_3}\)  i.e.  \(\mathrm{H_3C}-\mathrm{CH_3}\)

**c. \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\)** (ethene) — the two carbons have only \(4 + 4 + 4\times 1 = 12\) valence electrons between them, so a single C-C bond would leave each carbon short of an octet. The carbons therefore share **two** pairs, a double bond, and each carbon also carries two C-H bonds. No lone pairs.

\(\mathrm{H_2C}\!::\!\mathrm{CH_2}\)  i.e.  \(\mathrm{H_2C}=\mathrm{CH_2}\)

**d. \(\mathrm{CF_3Cl}\)** — carbon is the central atom (it is the least electronegative, which is the chapter's own rule for choosing the central atom). It forms four single bonds, one to each of the three fluorines and one to chlorine. Each halogen keeps three lone pairs; carbon has none and reaches its octet.

\(\mathrm{Cl}-\underset{\displaystyle \mathrm{F}}{\overset{\displaystyle \mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{F}\)  with three lone pairs on every halogen.

**e. \(\mathrm{SO_2}\)** — sulphur is the central atom with 6 valence electrons and each oxygen brings 6, so \(6 + 12 = 18\) electrons are to be placed. Two single S-O bonds leave sulphur short of an octet, so one multiple bond is formed, exactly as in the nitrite ion of Problem 5.1. Sulphur is left with one lone pair, which is why Table 5.4 classifies \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) as the \(\mathrm{AB_2E}\) type with a bent shape and a bond angle of \(119.3^\circ\).

\(\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}} = \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{S}} - \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}\!:\)  \(\leftrightarrow\)  \(:\!\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}} - \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{S}} = \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}\)

As with the nitrite ion, the two forms differ only in the position of the electrons and are canonical forms of one resonance hybrid (§5.8).

Both diagrams show the overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, which is a \(\sigma\) overlap (§5.4.3 i).

**a. Fluorine molecule \((\mathrm{F_2})\) — \(p\)-\(p\) \(\sigma\) overlap.**

The electronic configuration of fluorine is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^2\ 2p_y^2\ 2p_z^1}\), so each atom has exactly one half-filled orbital, the \(2p_z\). Taking \(z\) as the internuclear axis, the two \(2p_z\) orbitals approach end-on and overlap along that axis. The diagram is therefore two two-lobed \(p\) orbitals lying on the same line with their near lobes merged between the nuclei; the \(2p_x\) and \(2p_y\) orbitals are full and take no part.

\(\mathrm{F}(2p_z) + \mathrm{F}(2p_z) \longrightarrow \mathrm{F}-\mathrm{F}\)  (\(p\)-\(p\) \(\sigma\) bond)

**b. Hydrogen fluoride molecule \((\mathrm{HF})\) — \(s\)-\(p\) \(\sigma\) overlap.**

Hydrogen is \(\mathrm{1s^1}\) and fluorine is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^2\ 2p_y^2\ 2p_z^1}\). The half-filled spherical \(1s\) orbital of hydrogen overlaps along the internuclear axis with the half-filled \(2p_z\) orbital of fluorine. The diagram is therefore a sphere merging end-on into one lobe of a two-lobed \(p\) orbital.

\(\mathrm{H}(1s) + \mathrm{F}(2p_z) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{F}\)  (\(s\)-\(p\) \(\sigma\) bond)

In both cases the electrons in the two half-filled orbitals must have opposite spins, and the greater the extent of the overlap the stronger the bond formed (postulates ii and iv of §5.4.1). The book prints the item as "Hydrogen fluoxide molecule"; that is a misprint for hydrogen fluoride, \(\mathrm{HF}\), which is the molecule the chapter treats in §5.4.3 c.

| | Sigma \((\sigma)\) bond | Pi \((\pi)\) bond |
|---|---|---|
| Mode of overlap | The bonding orbitals overlap **along the internuclear axis** (axial or head-on overlap). | The two half-filled orbitals overlap **sideways (laterally)**, perpendicular to the internuclear axis. |
| Orbitals involved | \(s\)-\(s\), \(s\)-\(p\) or \(p\)-\(p\) (and hybrid orbitals), e.g. \(\mathrm{H_2}\), \(\mathrm{HF}\), \(\mathrm{F_2}\). | Only unhybridized parallel \(p\) orbitals, e.g. the second bond of \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\). |
| Extent of overlap | Large, because the orbitals meet end-on. | Small, because the orbitals only graze each other sideways. |
| Strength | Stronger — greater overlap means a stronger bond (postulate iv of §5.4.1). | Weaker than a \(\sigma\) bond. |
| Electron cloud | Concentrated between the two nuclei, symmetrical about the bond axis. | Concentrated above and below the bond axis, not on it. |
| Occurrence | A bond between two atoms is always a \(\sigma\) bond first; a single bond is purely \(\sigma\). | A \(\pi\) bond forms only in addition to a \(\sigma\) bond, i.e. only in double and triple bonds. |

Example: in acetylene the C-C triple bond is one \(\sigma\) bond plus two \(\pi\) bonds.

[Textbook misprint: the chapter gives the H-O-H bond angle THREE different values, and they cannot all be right. §5.3 prints \(104^\circ 35'\); Table 5.5, whose whole purpose is to list bond angles, prints \(104^\circ 28'\); and the table of Ex Q.6 prints \(104.5^\circ\) (which is \(104^\circ 30'\)). The three differ by up to 7 arc-minutes. Which one is the misprint cannot be settled from the chapter itself, so the answer below quotes \(104^\circ 35'\), the value the running text of §5.3 derives when it explains the reduction from the tetrahedral angle. Any of the three should be accepted.]

**Electron distribution around oxygen.** The oxygen atom has six electrons in its valence shell. On bond formation with two hydrogen atoms it has eight electrons in that shell — four of them, i.e. two pairs, are **bonded pairs** shared with the two hydrogens, and the other four, i.e. two pairs, remain on oxygen as **lone pairs**. In terms of valence bond theory the oxygen is \(sp^3\) hybridized, two of the four hybrid orbitals holding the O-H bonding pairs and the other two holding the lone pairs.

\(\mathrm{H}\!:\!\overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}\!:\!\mathrm{H}\)

**Shape.** Four electron pairs around the central atom would give a tetrahedral arrangement, but two of them are lone pairs, so the molecule belongs to the \(\mathrm{AB_2E_2}\) type of Table 5.4 and its shape is **angular (bent)**, not tetrahedral. The reason is the repulsion order \(\mathrm{L.P-L.P} > \mathrm{L.P-B.P} > \mathrm{B.P-B.P}\): the two lone pairs repel each other most strongly and push the two bonded pairs closer together.

**Bond angle.** The H-O-H angle is therefore reduced from the tetrahedral value of \(109^\circ 28'\) to \(104^\circ 35'\), the value §5.3 of this chapter gives for water.

**Octet rule.** The rule states that during the formation of a chemical bond an atom loses, gains or shares electrons so that its outermost orbit (valence shell) contains eight electrons, and the atom thereby attains the electronic configuration of the nearest inert gas. It rests on the stability of the noble gases, which have eight electrons \((ns^2 np^6)\) in the valence shell. It does not apply to H and Li, which tend to have only two electrons — a duplet, like helium.

The rule is useful in explaining the normal valence of elements and the combination of atoms into molecules, but §5.2.7 lists molecules whose central atom does **not** have eight valence electrons and which are nevertheless stable. Two such classes are:

**a. Incomplete octet.** Here the central atom has **fewer** than eight electrons in its valence shell and the molecule is still stable, so the rule cannot be a requirement for stability. Examples given by the chapter are \(\mathrm{BF_3}\), \(\mathrm{BeCl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{LiCl}\): lithium in \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) has only two electrons, beryllium in \(\mathrm{BeCl_2}\) has four, and boron in \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) has six electrons in the valence shell.

**b. Expanded octet.** Here the central atom has **more** than eight electrons around it. This is possible for elements of the third period and beyond, which have vacant \(d\) orbitals available. The chapter's examples are \(\mathrm{SF_6}\), \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) — sulphur has 12 electrons around it in \(\mathrm{SF_6}\) and in \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\), and phosphorus has 10 in \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\). The chapter adds that the same element may still obey the rule elsewhere: in \(\mathrm{SCl_2}\) sulphur has eight electrons around it.

(The chapter lists a third limitation of the same kind, odd-electron molecules such as \(\mathrm{NO}\) and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\), and further limitations of the rule: it cannot explain the observed shape and geometry of a molecule, nor the difference in energies and reactivities of molecules whose bonds are all formed in the same way.)

The book prints "octel" for octet and "inadequecies" for inadequacies in this question.

**a. Ionic bond.** When one atom transfers one or more electrons to another, both attain a stable noble-gas configuration and become oppositely charged ions; the strong electrostatic force of attraction that then holds the two ions together is an ionic (electrovalent) bond. It forms between an element of low ionization enthalpy and one with a high negative electron gain enthalpy.

*Example (§5.2.1).* Sodium \((2,8,1)\) has one valence electron and loses it to reach the neon configuration; chlorine \((2,8,7)\) is one short of argon and gains it.

\(\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{Cl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{\oplus} + \mathrm{Cl}^{\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{\oplus}\mathrm{Cl}^{\ominus}\ (\mathrm{NaCl})\)

**b. Covalent bond.** The attractive force which exists due to the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms of similar electronegativity, or having a small difference in electronegativities, is called a covalent bond. Each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair and has an equal claim on it, and the shared pair is written as a dash.

*Example (§5.2.3).* Two hydrogen atoms, each \(\mathrm{1s^1}\), share their valence electrons:

\(\mathrm{H} + \mathrm{H} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}\!:\!\mathrm{H}\)  or  \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}\)

Each hydrogen thereby attains the helium duplet. Similarly two chlorine atoms share one pair to give \(\mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Cl}\), each attaining the argon octet.

**c. Co-ordinate bond.** This chapter mentions the co-ordinate covalent bond only once, in limitation (i) of §5.4.7, where it is described as a bond "in which both the electrons are contributed by one of the bonded atoms" — the donor supplies the whole shared pair and the acceptor supplies an empty orbital. Once formed it is indistinguishable from an ordinary covalent bond. **The chapter gives no worked example of one**, so the example below is supplied from outside it: in the ammonium ion, the lone pair on nitrogen in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is donated to a proton \(\mathrm{H}^{\oplus}\), which brings no electron of its own, giving \(\mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}}\) — the species the chapter itself prints as an example of formal charge.

Hybridization was introduced because plain valence bond theory, which says that the number of bonds an atom can form equals the number of unpaired electrons in its valence shell, fails on two counts (§5.4.4):

**1. It cannot explain the observed valency.** Beryllium is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2}\) with no unpaired electron, yet it forms two bonds; boron \((\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^1})\) has one unpaired electron yet shows a valency of three; carbon \((\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^1\ 2p_y^1})\) has two, yet is tetravalent. Promoting one \(2s\) electron to a vacant \(2p\) orbital gives Be, B and C two, three and four half-filled orbitals respectively and accounts for the numbers.

**2. Promotion alone still cannot explain that all the bonds are equivalent.** In \(\mathrm{BeF_2}\), an excited beryllium would use one \(s\) and one \(p\) orbital, so the molecule would contain one \(s\)-\(p\) bond and one \(p\)-\(p\) bond, of unequal strength — but both Be-F bonds are found to be identical. The same difficulty arises in \(\mathrm{BF_3}\), \(\mathrm{BH_3}\), \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) and \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\): in methane the overlaps would be of \(s\), \(p_x\), \(p_y\) and \(p_z\) with hydrogen \(1s\), yet experimentally all four C-H bond lengths, bond strengths and bond angles are identical.

Hybridization removes the difficulty. It is the mixing of valence orbitals of the **same** atom and their recasting into an equal number of new, equivalent orbitals — hybrid orbitals — which have the same energy and shape and are oriented in space so that repulsion is minimum. Because the hybrid orbitals are identical, the bonds they form are identical, and because they are directional with one large lobe they overlap better and give bonds stronger than those formed by pure orbitals. Hybridization therefore explains both the observed valency and the observed shapes and equal bond parameters of molecules.

**Ground state and excitation.** The ground state configuration of carbon is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^1\ 2p_y^1\ 2p_z^0}\), which has only two unpaired electrons. To form four equivalent bonds with hydrogen, one electron from the \(2s\) orbital is excited to the vacant \(2p_z\) orbital, leaving four half-filled orbitals: \(2s,\ 2p_x,\ 2p_y,\ 2p_z\).

**Hybridization.** These four orbitals, being of comparable energy and on the same atom, mix and are recast into **four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals** of the same shape and equal energy, each containing one unpaired electron. Each hybrid has one large lobe and one small lobe.

**Orientation.** The four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals arrange themselves as far apart as possible, so that repulsion between them is minimum. They therefore point towards the four corners of a regular tetrahedron and make an angle of \(109^\circ 28'\) with one another.

**Bond formation.** Each \(sp^3\) hybrid orbital, with its one electron, overlaps axially with the \(1s\) orbital of a hydrogen atom whose electron has the opposite spin. This gives four C-H \(\sigma\) bonds of the \(sp^3\)-\(s\) type.

**Geometry.** Because the four hybrid orbitals are equivalent and tetrahedrally disposed, the four C-H bonds are of identical length and strength and the \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) molecule is **tetrahedral**, with all H-C-H bond angles equal to \(109^\circ 28'\). This is exactly what experiment finds, and it is what pure \(s\) and \(p\) orbitals could not have explained.

In both molecules the central atom is \(sp^3\) hybridized, so in both the four electron pairs are arranged tetrahedrally and the **expected** bond angle is \(109^\circ 28'\). What differs is the **number of lone pairs**, and lone pairs do not repel in the same way as bonded pairs.

The chapter's rule (§5.3) is

\(\mathrm{L.P-L.P} > \mathrm{L.P-B.P} > \mathrm{B.P-B.P}\)

Lone pair-lone pair repulsion is the strongest because a lone pair is under the influence of only one nucleus and so spreads out, while a bonded pair is shared between two nuclei and is drawn in.

**Ammonia.** Nitrogen has eight electrons in its valence shell, six of them forming three N-H bonds and the remaining pair a single lone pair. The stronger lone pair-bond pair repulsions push the three bonded pairs inwards, so the angle falls from \(109^\circ 28'\) to about \(107^\circ\) and the shape becomes trigonal pyramidal.

**Water.** Oxygen has two bonded pairs and **two** lone pairs. Now there is lone pair-lone pair repulsion as well, which is stronger still; the two lone pairs are pushed towards the bonded pairs and the bond pair-lone pair repulsion becomes stronger than in ammonia. The angle is therefore squeezed further, to \(104^\circ 35'\), and the geometry is angular.

So the order of the angles, \(109^\circ 28' > 107^\circ > 104^\circ 35'\), simply follows the number of lone pairs on the central atom: none in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), one in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), two in \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). The same \(sp^3\) hybridization is consistent with all three.

**a. Sigma \((\sigma)\) bond is stronger than pi \((\pi)\) bond.**

Postulate (iv) of valence bond theory says that the greater the extent of overlap, the stronger the bond formed. A \(\sigma\) bond is formed when the two orbitals overlap **along the internuclear axis**, so they meet head-on and the overlap is large, with the electron cloud concentrated directly between the two nuclei. A \(\pi\) bond is formed when two parallel \(p\) orbitals overlap **sideways**, perpendicular to the internuclear axis; that lateral overlap is much smaller and the electron cloud lies above and below the axis rather than between the nuclei, so it binds them less effectively. Hence the \(\sigma\) bond is the stronger of the two.

**b. HF is a polar molecule.**

Section 5.6.5 states that when a covalent bond is formed between atoms of different elements with different electronegativities, the shared electron pair is not situated midway but is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, separating the charge. Fluorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pair lies closer to fluorine; fluorine acquires a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge,

\(\delta^{+}\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{F}^{\delta-}\)

and the bond is a polar covalent bond. Since \(\mathrm{HF}\) is a diatomic molecule there is only this one bond dipole and nothing to cancel it, so the molecular dipole moment is non-zero — Table 5.8 gives \(\mu = 1.91\ \mathrm{D}\), and the chapter marks the crossed arrow on the structure to show the shift of electron density towards fluorine. \(\mathrm{HF}\) is therefore polar.

**c. Carbon is tetravalent in nature.**

The ground state configuration of carbon, \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^1\ 2p_y^1\ 2p_z^0}\), contains only two unpaired electrons and would predict a valency of two. But the \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals differ only slightly in energy, so one \(2s\) electron is promoted (uncoupled) into the vacant \(2p_z\) orbital, giving the excited configuration \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^1\ 2p_x^1\ 2p_y^1\ 2p_z^1}\) with **four** half-filled orbitals. Postulate (v) of §5.4.1 says the number of bonds formed equals the number of half-filled valence orbitals, so carbon can form four bonds. These four orbitals then hybridize to four equivalent \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals, which is why all four bonds in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) and \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) are of identical length and strength.

[Textbook note (not an error): the chapter states the H-N-H bond angle of ammonia two ways — §5.3 gives \(107^\circ 18'\) when it explains the reduction from the tetrahedral value, while Table 5.5 lists it simply as 107 (that table prints no degree symbol on any of its three entries). The answer below uses the rounded \(107^\circ\), which is also the value printed in the stem of Ex Q.3 (G).]

**Hybridization.** The nitrogen atom in ammonia is \(sp^3\) hybridized: one \(2s\) and the three \(2p\) orbitals mix and recast into four equivalent \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals directed towards the corners of a tetrahedron. Three of these hybrid orbitals are half-filled and overlap axially with the \(1s\) orbitals of three hydrogen atoms to give three N-H \(\sigma\) bonds; the fourth hybrid orbital holds nitrogen's **lone pair**.

**Geometry.** The arrangement of the four electron pairs is tetrahedral, but only three of the four positions carry an atom. The molecule therefore belongs to the \(\mathrm{AB_3E}\) type of Table 5.4 and its shape is **trigonal pyramidal** — the nitrogen at the apex and the three hydrogens forming the triangular base.

**Bond angle.** Because lone pair-bond pair repulsion is stronger than bond pair-bond pair repulsion, the lone pair pushes the three bonded pairs inwards and the H-N-H angle is reduced from the tetrahedral \(109^\circ 28'\) to about \(107^\circ\), the value listed in Table 5.5.

All three are \(\sigma\) overlaps — the orbitals meet along the internuclear axis — but they differ in which orbitals are involved (§5.4.3 i).

**a. \(\mathrm{H_2}\) — \(s\)-\(s\) overlap.** Hydrogen is \(\mathrm{1s^1}\). The two half-filled, spherical \(1s\) orbitals approach each other and overlap along the internuclear axis to form a \(\sigma\) bond. Diagrammatically: two spheres merging where they meet, the shared electron cloud lying between the nuclei.

**b. \(\mathrm{F_2}\) — \(p\)-\(p\) overlap.** Fluorine is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^2\ 2p_y^2\ 2p_z^1}\), so the only half-filled orbital is \(2p_z\). Taking \(z\) as the internuclear axis, the \(2p_z\) orbitals of the two atoms meet end-on and overlap along that axis, giving a \(p\)-\(p\) \(\sigma\) bond. Diagrammatically: two dumb-bell shaped orbitals lying on one line, their facing lobes merged.

**c. \(\mathrm{H-F}\) — \(s\)-\(p\) overlap.** Here one half-filled \(s\) orbital of hydrogen \((1s^1)\) and one half-filled \(p\) orbital of fluorine \((2p_z^1)\) overlap along the internuclear axis, giving an \(s\)-\(p\) \(\sigma\) bond. Diagrammatically: a sphere merging end-on with one lobe of a dumb-bell.

In each case the two electrons must have opposite spins, which get neutralized on overlapping, and the greater the overlap the stronger the resulting bond. Note that a lateral (side-by-side) overlap of two \(p\) orbitals would instead give a \(\pi\) bond, which is not what happens in any of these three molecules.

The difference is not in the hybridization alone but in the number of **lone pairs** on the central atom, which by VSEPR also help to decide the shape.

**\(\mathrm{BeF_2}\).** Beryllium is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^0}\). One \(2s\) electron is promoted to a \(2p\) orbital, and the \(2s\) and one \(2p\) orbital then undergo \(sp\) hybridization to give two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals. Two \(sp\) hybrids repel each other least when they point in exactly opposite directions, so they are oriented at \(180^\circ\). Both are used in bonding to the two fluorine atoms and **beryllium is left with no lone pair**, so nothing distorts the arrangement. There are only two electron pairs around the central atom, which is the linear case of Table 5.3. Hence F-Be-F is linear with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

**\(\mathrm{H_2O}\).** Oxygen has six valence electrons; after forming two O-H bonds there are eight electrons, i.e. **four** pairs, around it — two bonded pairs and two lone pairs. Four pairs adopt a tetrahedral arrangement, so the two O-H bonds cannot be opposite each other. Furthermore the lone pairs repel more strongly than the bonded pairs \((\mathrm{L.P-L.P} > \mathrm{L.P-B.P} > \mathrm{B.P-B.P})\) and squeeze the two bonded pairs together, reducing the angle from \(109^\circ 28'\) to \(104^\circ 35'\). The molecule is the \(\mathrm{AB_2E_2}\) type of Table 5.4 and is therefore angular.

In short: two bonded pairs and no lone pair give a linear molecule; two bonded pairs with two lone pairs give an angular one.

Again the deciding factor is the lone pair on the central atom.

**\(\mathrm{BF_3}\) is trigonal planar.** The ground state of boron is \(\mathrm{1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p_x^1}\). One \(2s\) electron is uncoupled and promoted to a vacant \(2p\) orbital, and the \(2s\) and two \(2p\) orbitals then undergo \(sp^2\) hybridization, giving three \(sp^2\) hybrid orbitals of equal energy. Three equivalent orbitals repel one another least when they lie **in one plane** pointing to the corners of an equilateral triangle at \(120^\circ\). Each overlaps axially with a half-filled \(2p_z\) orbital of a fluorine atom to give three B-F \(\sigma\) bonds. Boron is left with **no lone pair**, so nothing distorts the triangle: every F-B-F angle is \(120^\circ\) and the molecule is trigonal planar. (This is also an incomplete-octet molecule — boron ends with only six electrons in its valence shell.)

**\(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is pyramidal.** Nitrogen is \(sp^3\) hybridized, giving **four** hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally. Three of them form N-H \(\sigma\) bonds and the fourth holds a **lone pair**. Since a lone pair occupies one corner of the tetrahedron, the three hydrogens cannot lie in the same plane as the nitrogen — they form a triangular base with the nitrogen above it, which is the \(\mathrm{AB_3E}\) trigonal pyramidal type of Table 5.4. The stronger lone pair-bond pair repulsion also pushes the bonds inwards, reducing the angle from \(109^\circ 28'\) to about \(107^\circ\).

So three bonded pairs with **no** lone pair give a planar molecule \((sp^2,\ 120^\circ)\), while three bonded pairs with **one** lone pair give a pyramidal one \((sp^3,\ \approx 107^\circ)\).

Acetylene is \(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-H}\), in which each carbon atom is \(sp\) hybridized: one \(s\) and one \(p\) orbital mix and recast into two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals set at \(180^\circ\), while the other two \(p\) orbitals remain unhybridized and at right angles to the hybrids.

**a. Number of covalent bonds formed — five.** Of the two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals on each carbon, one overlaps axially with the \(1s\) orbital of a hydrogen atom and the other overlaps axially with the \(sp\) hybrid orbital of the second carbon. The remaining two unhybridized \(p\) orbitals on each carbon overlap laterally in pairs, giving two more bonds. So there are two C-H bonds and three C-C bonds, five covalent bonds in all.

**b. Number of sigma and pi bonds — three \(\sigma\) and two \(\pi\).**

| Bond | Type | Formed by |
|---|---|---|
| 2 C-H | \(\sigma\) | \(sp\)-\(s\) axial overlap |
| 1 C-C | \(\sigma\) | \(sp\)-\(sp\) axial overlap |
| 2 C-C | \(\pi\) | \(p\)-\(p\) lateral overlap |

The carbon-carbon triple bond is thus one \(\sigma\) bond and two \(\pi\) bonds, which is the count the chapter also prints in the exercise table: \((3\sigma + 2\pi)\).

**c. Type of hybridization — \(sp\).** Since the two \(sp\) hybrids on each carbon are at \(180^\circ\), all four atoms lie on a straight line and the molecule is linear.

(The book prints "covalend" for covalent in this question.)

**a. Bond Enthalpy.** The amount of energy required to break one mole of bond of one type, present between two atoms in the gaseous state, is termed the bond enthalpy. For a diatomic molecule the bond dissociation energy is the same as the bond enthalpy — for example the bond enthalpy of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is \(435.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), and that of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is \(431.0\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). For a polyatomic molecule the two are not identical: the bond enthalpy is then the **average** of the successive bond dissociation energies. In water,

\(\mathrm{H_2O(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H(g)} + \mathrm{OH(g)},\quad \Delta H_1 = 502\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\mathrm{OH(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H(g)} + \mathrm{O(g)},\quad \Delta H_2 = 427\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\Delta_a H = \dfrac{502 + 427}{2} = 464.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Bond enthalpy is a measure of the strength of the bond: the larger it is, the stronger the bond.

**b. Bond Length.** Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two covalently bonded atoms in a molecule. It is measured by X-ray and electron diffraction techniques and is expressed in picometre \((\mathrm{pm})\) or in angstrom \((\mathrm{\mathring{A}})\). Each atom of the bonded pair contributes to it, so bond length increases with the size of the atoms and decreases as the multiplicity of the bond increases — hence a C-C single bond \((154\ \mathrm{pm})\) is longer than \(\mathrm{C=C}\ (133\ \mathrm{pm})\), which is longer than \(\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}\ (120\ \mathrm{pm})\).

Count the bonded pairs and lone pairs on the central atom, then read the shape from Tables 5.3 and 5.4.

**a. \(\mathrm{CF_4}\)** — carbon has four valence electrons, all four used in bonding to four fluorine atoms: **4 bonded pairs, 0 lone pairs**. That is the four-electron-pair case of Table 5.3, so the shape is **tetrahedral** and the F-C-F bond angle is \(109^\circ 28'\), exactly as in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\).

**b. \(\mathrm{NF_3}\)** — nitrogen has five valence electrons; three form N-F bonds and the remaining two are a lone pair: **3 bonded pairs, 1 lone pair**. This is the \(\mathrm{AB_3E}\) type of Table 5.4, so the shape is **trigonal pyramidal**, like \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{PCl_3}\). Lone pair-bond pair repulsion reduces the angle below the tetrahedral \(109^\circ 28'\); the chapter gives \(107^\circ\) for the analogous \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) but **does not print a value for \(\mathrm{NF_3}\)**, so all that can be stated on the chapter's evidence is that the F-N-F angle is somewhat less than \(109^\circ 28'\).

**c. \(\mathrm{HCN}\)** — carbon is the central atom, joined to hydrogen by a single bond and to nitrogen by a triple bond. A multiple bond counts as one region of electron density, so carbon has **2 bonded regions and 0 lone pairs**. That is the two-electron-pair case of Table 5.3, so the molecule is **linear** with an H-C-N bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

**d. \(\mathrm{H_2S}\)** — sulphur has six valence electrons; two form S-H bonds and four remain as two lone pairs: **2 bonded pairs, 2 lone pairs**. This is the \(\mathrm{AB_2E_2}\) type, in which Table 5.4 names \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) explicitly, so the shape is **bent (angular)**, as Table 5.8 also records. Two lone pairs squeeze the bonded pairs, so the H-S-H angle is well below the tetrahedral value; the chapter gives \(104^\circ 35'\) for the analogous \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) but **prints no angle for \(\mathrm{H_2S}\)**.

The bond length **decreases** as unsaturation increases.

Reading the table across the carbon-carbon bond: ethane (single bond) \(0.154\ \mathrm{nm}\), ethene (double bond) \(0.134\ \mathrm{nm}\), ethyne (triple bond) \(0.120\ \mathrm{nm}\). Going from a single to a double to a triple bond the length falls by \(0.020\ \mathrm{nm}\) and then by a further \(0.014\ \mathrm{nm}\).

The reason is given in §5.6.3: bond length depends on the size of the atoms and on the **multiplicity** of the bond, and it decreases as the multiplicity increases. More shared pairs between the same two carbon atoms means a stronger attraction pulling the nuclei closer together, so the equilibrium internuclear distance is shorter.

On the evidence of this table the most stable compound is **ethyne, \(\mathrm{C_2H_2}\)**.

The table's last row gives the bond enthalpies of the carbon-carbon bond: \(348\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for ethane, \(612\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for ethene and \(837\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for ethyne. Section 5.6.2 states that the larger the bond dissociation energy, the stronger the bond in the molecule, and §5.6.4 adds that stabilities of molecules can be determined by knowing the bond order — as bond order increases, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases. Ethyne has the highest bond order (three), the largest bond enthalpy \((837\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}})\) and the shortest bond \((0.120\ \mathrm{nm})\), so its carbon-carbon bond is the strongest and hardest to break of the three.

One qualification, since the question is answered from this table alone: what the table compares is the strength of the **carbon-carbon bond**, not the overall chemical reactivity of the three compounds towards reagents.

Bond strength and bond enthalpy are **directly related**: the greater the bond enthalpy, the stronger the bond.

Bond enthalpy is defined (§5.6.2) as the energy required to break one mole of that bond in the gaseous state, so it is a direct measure of how firmly the two atoms are held together — the chapter states that "the bond enthalpy is a measure of strength of the bond between two atoms" and that "larger is the bond dissociation energy stronger is the bond in the molecule".

The table bears this out: the carbon-carbon bond enthalpy rises \(348 \rightarrow 612 \rightarrow 837\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) from ethane to ethene to ethyne, and in the same order the bond goes from single to double to triple, i.e. from weakest to strongest.

The three quantities move together in a single consistent pattern, with bond length running opposite to the other two.

**As the multiplicity (bond order) of the carbon-carbon bond increases:**

| | Ethane (single) | Ethene (double) | Ethyne (triple) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bond length (nm) | 0.154 | 0.134 | 0.120 |
| Bond enthalpy \((\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}})\) | 348 | 612 | 837 |

- **Bond length decreases** — more shared pairs pull the two nuclei closer (§5.6.3).
- **Bond enthalpy increases** — more energy is needed to break the bond (§5.6.4: as bond order increases, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases).
- **Bond strength increases**, because bond enthalpy is the measure of bond strength (§5.6.2).
- **Stability of the bond increases**, since a stronger bond is harder to break.

So the overall relation is: **the shorter the bond, the larger its bond enthalpy, the stronger it is and the more stable it is.** Bond length is inversely related to bond enthalpy, bond strength and stability, while those three vary in the same direction as one another.

**Row 2, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).** The structural formula \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\) and the shape "Linear" are given, so the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and the missing bond angle is that of a linear molecule, \(180^\circ\). The stability of an ionic compound is measured by its **lattice enthalpy** — the energy released when the gaseous ions come together to form one mole of the solid (equivalently, the energy required to separate one mole of the solid completely into its gaseous ions).

Section 5.2.2 puts it explicitly: the conversion \(\mathrm{NaCl(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) releases \(788\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), far more than the energy absorbed in forming the ions, and "thus stability of an ionic compound can be estimated by knowing the amount of energy released during lattice formation and not just by energy associated with completion of octet around the ionic species in the gaseous state alone". The larger the lattice enthalpy, the more stable the ionic solid.

(The book prints "stalility" for stability in this question.)

Reading the lattice enthalpy values straight from Table 5.1 of this chapter:

| Compound | Lattice enthalpy \((\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}})\) |
|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) | 5492 |
| \(\mathrm{BeF_2}\) | 3020 |
| \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) | 2258 |
| \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) | 853 |
| \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) | 788 |

The decreasing (descending) order of lattice energies is therefore

\(\mathrm{AlCl_3} > \mathrm{BeF_2} > \mathrm{CaCl_2} > \mathrm{LiCl} > \mathrm{NaCl}\)

The order follows the two rules the chapter states immediately below that table. First, for the same anion, cations of higher charge give larger lattice energies — hence \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}} > \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} > \mathrm{Na^{+}}\) among the chlorides, which is the chapter's own example \(\mathrm{AlCl_3 > CaCl_2 > NaCl}\). Second, as the size of the cation decreases the lattice energy increases — hence \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) exceeds \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), the lithium ion being the smaller. \(\mathrm{BeF_2}\) is high on the list because it combines a doubly-charged and very small \(\mathrm{Be^{2+}}\) ion with the small \(\mathrm{F^-}\) ion.

There are **12 electrons** around sulphur in \(\mathrm{SF_6}\).

Sulphur forms six S-F single bonds, each a shared pair, so \(6 \times 2 = 12\) electrons surround the sulphur atom and it has no lone pair left. This is more than eight, so \(\mathrm{SF_6}\) is one of the chapter's expanded-octet molecules (§5.2.7 ii, where \(\mathrm{SF_6}\), \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) are listed as having more than eight electrons around the central atom); the caption under the figure on that page reads "\(\mathrm{SF_6}\); 12 electrons around sulfur". Sulphur can do this because, being a third-period element, it has vacant \(d\) orbitals available. The chapter adds that sulphur still obeys the octet rule elsewhere — in \(\mathrm{SCl_2}\) it has eight electrons around it.

A covalent bond is formed by the **overlap of atomic orbitals**, and most atomic orbitals have a definite orientation in space, so the bond can only form along particular directions.

Postulate (viii) of §5.4.1 states it: the \(s\) orbital, being spherical, can overlap in any direction, but the \(p\) orbitals can overlap **only in the \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\) directions**, and \(d\) and \(f\) orbitals are likewise oriented in certain directions in space and overlap only in those directions. Since the bond forms where the overlap is greatest, and the greatest overlap occurs only along those axes, the resulting covalent bond points in a fixed direction — the chapter concludes, "Thus the covalent bond is directional in nature."

This directional character is what gives covalent molecules definite shapes and bond angles: \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) is tetrahedral with \(109^\circ 28'\) angles and \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) trigonal planar with \(120^\circ\) angles, whereas an ionic bond, being a non-directional electrostatic attraction, imposes no such shape.

(The book prints "Covalant" for covalent in this question.)

The forces at work during the formation of a molecule are the **electrostatic attractions and repulsions between the nuclei and the electrons of the two combining atoms** (§5.4.2).

When two atoms A and B approach each other, two kinds of interaction develop:

- **Attractive forces** — between the nucleus of one atom and the electrons of the other (nucleus of A with electrons of B, and nucleus of B with electrons of A). These lower the energy of the system.
- **Repulsive forces** — between the two nuclei, and between the electrons of one atom and those of the other. These raise the energy of the system.

The balance between them decides whether a bond forms. When the newly developed attractive forces contribute more than the newly developed repulsive forces, the potential energy of the system falls, overlap of the two half-filled orbitals takes place and a bond is formed. The atoms approach only up to the distance at which the attractive and repulsive forces exactly balance; there the energy is minimum and the stability maximum, and that separation is the bond length. Pushing the atoms closer still makes the repulsions dominate and the energy rise again.

A pi \((\pi)\) bond is formed by **lateral (sideways) overlap of two half-filled \(p\) orbitals**, the overlap being perpendicular to the internuclear axis.

Section 5.4.3 (ii) defines it: "When two half filled orbitals of two atoms overlap side ways (laterally) it is called \(\pi\) overlap and it is perpendicular to the internuclear axis." The two \(p\) orbitals concerned must be parallel to each other and unhybridized, and the electron cloud of the resulting bond lies above and below the internuclear axis rather than along it. Because that sideways overlap is smaller than the head-on overlap of a \(\sigma\) bond, a \(\pi\) bond is the weaker of the two.

Example: the second bond of the \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond in ethene is a \(p\)-\(p\) \(\pi\) bond formed by the lateral overlap of the unhybridized \(p\) orbitals left on the two \(sp^2\) carbons.

Section 5.4.4 gives **two** steps in hybridization:

**i. Formation of the excited state.** The paired electrons in the ground state are uncoupled and one electron is promoted to a vacant orbital of slightly higher energy, so that the total number of half-filled orbitals becomes equal to the valency of the element in the stable compound. For example in \(\mathrm{BeF_2}\) the valency of beryllium is two, so one electron from the \(2s\) orbital is uncoupled and promoted to a \(2p\) orbital.

**ii. Mixing and recasting of orbitals.** The \(s\) and \(p\) orbitals, which have slightly different energies, now mix with each other; a redistribution of electron density and energy takes place and new orbitals of exactly the same shape and energy are formed. These new hybrid orbitals then arrange themselves in space so that there is minimum repulsion and maximum separation between them — which is why the two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals of beryllium end up at \(180^\circ\).

Two conditions must be met: only orbitals belonging to the **same atom** can hybridize, and they must have **nearly the same energy** (so \(2s\) and \(2p\) hybridize but \(3s\) and \(2p\) do not).

The bond order of a molecule is calculated from the number of electrons in its bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals (§5.5.4 c):

\(\text{Bond order} = \dfrac{N_b - N_a}{2}\)

where \(N_b\) is the number of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and \(N_a\) the number in antibonding molecular orbitals.

Applied to the chapter's own examples: \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gives \((2-0)/2 = 1\); \(\mathrm{Li_2}\) gives \((4-2)/2 = 1\); \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gives \((10-4)/2 = 3\); \(\mathrm{O_2}\) gives \((10-6)/2 = 2\); and \(\mathrm{F_2}\) gives \((10-8)/2 = 1\). A molecule is stable when the number of bonding electrons exceeds the number of antibonding electrons, i.e. when the bond order is positive.

Because the \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecule contains **two unpaired electrons**, one in each of the two \(\pi^*\) antibonding molecular orbitals.

Oxygen has 8 electrons per atom, so the molecule has 16. Filling the molecular orbitals in order of increasing energy gives

\((\sigma 1s)^2 (\sigma^* 1s)^2 (\sigma 2s)^2 (\sigma^* 2s)^2 (\sigma 2p_z)^2 (\pi 2p_x)^2 (\pi 2p_y)^2 (\pi^* 2p_x)^1 (\pi^* 2p_y)^1\)

The last two electrons go one into each of the degenerate \(\pi^* 2p_x\) and \(\pi^* 2p_y\) orbitals, leaving both half-filled. Section 5.5.4 (b) states that if all the molecular orbitals are completely filled the molecule is diamagnetic, but "if at least one MO is half filled (having one electron), the molecule is paramagnetic" — attracted by a magnetic field. \(\mathrm{O_2}\) has two such half-filled orbitals, so it is paramagnetic.

This is a case where molecular orbital theory succeeds and valence bond theory fails: §5.4.7 (ii) notes that on VBT oxygen would be expected to be diamagnetic, with no unpaired electrons at all.

**Formal charge.** Formal charge is the charge assigned to an atom in a molecule on the assumption that all the electrons are shared **equally** between the bonded atoms, regardless of their relative electronegativities. It is calculated from the Lewis structure as

\(\mathrm{FC} = \begin{pmatrix}\text{total no. of valence}\\ \text{electrons in the free atom}\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}\text{total no. of non-bonding}\\ \text{(lone pair) electrons}\end{pmatrix} - \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\text{total no. of bonding}\\ \text{(shared) electrons}\end{pmatrix}\)

or, in the chapter's short form, \(\mathrm{FC} = \mathrm{V.E} - \mathrm{N.E} - (\mathrm{B.E}/2)\).

**Significance.** A polyatomic molecule or ion can often be written as more than one Lewis structure, and formal charges are what let us choose between them: the structure having the lowest formal charges — as close to zero as possible — has the lowest energy and is the best representation.

**Example (the chapter's own \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) case).** Carbon dioxide can be written three ways:

- **A**, \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\) : \(\mathrm{FC(C)} = 4 - 0 - \tfrac{1}{2}(8) = 0\); each oxygen \(= 6 - 4 - \tfrac{1}{2}(4) = 0\).
- **B**, \(\mathrm{O} \equiv \mathrm{C} - \mathrm{O}\) : \(\mathrm{FC(C)} = 0\), but one oxygen is \(+1\) and the other \(-1\).
- **C**, \(\mathrm{O} - \mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{O}\) : again \(\mathrm{FC(C)} = 0\) with oxygens \(-1\) and \(+1\).

In structure A the formal charge on every atom is zero, whereas B and C carry separated \(+1\) and \(-1\) charges. Structure A therefore has the lowest energy and is the structure that best represents \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).
